Alabama shad (Alosa alabamae) is an anadromous clupeid that undertakes extensive spawning migrations from the Gulf of Mexico into the freshwater reaches of the Mobile River basin and adjacent drainages. Fertilised eggs are broadcast into the water column, where they drift as pelagic, yolk-laden embryos until hatching occurs. The recently emerged yolk-sac larva is minute and entirely lecithotrophic, relying on endogenous reserves until the onset of exogenous feeding. Based on the egg diameter of approximately 1 mm, which is comparable to that reported for the congeneric hickory shad (Alosa mediocris), the wet weight at birth is estimated at 0.000523 g [Wwb = estimated at 0.000523 g], a value that underscores the diminutive size of the prolarva at the moment of chorion rupture. This extremely low initial mass imposes a tight constraint on the duration of the endotrophic phase, as the larva must transition to active feeding before its finite yolk supply is exhausted, and the brief period of endogenous nutrition typically spans only a few days at typical river temperatures.

Juvenile and sub-adult Alabama shad feed voraciously on zooplankton and aquatic insects during their riverine residency, accumulating somatic tissue before their first downstream migration into estuarine and coastal waters. Growth during this period is rapid, and individuals attain a total length of approximately 38 cm [Lp = approximately 38 cm] at the onset of gonadal maturation. This length at puberty corresponds closely to the age at which the reproductive axis becomes fully functional, typically after about three years of growth in the wild. The attainment of sexual maturity at this moderate body size is consistent with the broader life-history strategy of iteroparous anadromous alosines, which balance the energetic demands of spawning migrations against the need for continued somatic growth across multiple reproductive seasons. Field collections have documented that sexually mature individuals of this species rarely exceed a very specific maximum length.

Comparative morphometric studies based on standard length measurements indicate that the ultimate total length of Alabama shad reaches approximately 60.7 cm [Li = approximately 60.7 cm], a figure derived from a standard length of 51 cm adjusted by a proportionality factor of 0.84. This asymptotic body size ranks among the midsized members of the genus Alosa, falling below the maximum lengths attained by the American shad (Alosa sapidissima) but exceeding those of many riverine alosines of similar trophic ecology. The largest individuals are typically females, a pattern that likely reflects the selective advantage of increased fecundity with body size in a species that produces pelagic eggs. Post-reproductive adults that survive the physiological stress of spawning may return to the Gulf for somatic recovery during the warmer months, though repeated annual migrations are not universally documented across all studied populations.

The lifespan of Alabama shad under natural thermal regimes has been inferred from mark-recapture studies and otolith annuli analysis, which suggest that individuals can survive for up to four years [am = up to four years] in the wild at the average water temperatures experienced throughout th at a temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]eir range. Laboratory holding experiments conducted at a constant temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C] have corroborated this estimate, showing that senescent mortality typically intervenes after approximately 1,460 days [am = approximately 1,460 days] under such conditions. This maximum longevity is comparatively short even among iteroparous anadromous clupeids, many of which can exceed six years of age. The relatively compressed lifespan of Alabama shad may be linked to the elevated metabolic costs associated with long-distance spawning migrations and the warm, productive waters of its subtropical habitat, which accelerate physiological aging.

Population-level assessments of Alabama shad have become a conservation priority, as historical declines in spawning habitat and the construction of migratory barriers have fragmented the species' distribution within its native drainages. Spawning adults ascend river reaches during the spring freshet, and successful reproduction depends upon the availability of clean gravel substrates and sufficient flow regimes to transport the pelagic eggs downstream. The exceptionally low mass of 0.000523 g [Wwb = 0.000523 g] at hatching renders the early larval stages acutely susceptible to environmental stressors such as entrainment in industrial water intakes and predation by planktivorous fishes that co-occur in the same riverine habitats. Conservation efforts have focused on restoring passage at dams and on maintaining minimum flow requirements to ensure that the brief larval period is completed before the yolk-sac is fully absorbed and exogenous food resources become critical for survival.
